findings.evidence: This relationship is documented in the Tri-County Library Data Cooperative's 2023 fines-elimination research brief, which reviewed return-rate data from fourteen library systems that eliminated fines between 2017 and 2022.
findings.fix: Name a source independent of the pilot itself that backs the participation/avoidance half of the principle (e.g., the Tri-County brief's own avoidance or usage figures, if it has any, or a separate citation), or narrow the warrant's claim to the return-rate effect the brief actually documents.
findings.location: Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide section, second paragraph
findings.violation: TOULMIN-BACKING is breached for the 'overall program participation' half of the general principle stated just before this sentence: the cited brief is named as backing, but by the artifact's own description it reviewed only 'return-rate data', not participation or fear-of-avoidance data, so the participation half of the principle has no independent backing beyond the single pilot's own survey, which is also the grounds the principle is being used to generalize.

findings.evidence: Consortium finance records show fine revenue covered under 2 percent of the annual materials budget over the last three fiscal years, and the four pilot branches absorbed the loss without a measurable change to their replacement-copy spending
findings.fix: Reconcile the branch count: state consistently whether the pilot covered four or five branches, and if the revenue-absorption data comes from a subset of the pilot branches, say which subset and why.
findings.location: Addressing the Revenue Concern section, second paragraph
findings.violation: TOULMIN-GROUNDS is breached because this evidence refers to 'the four pilot branches', while 'What the Pilot Showed' states the pilot ran 'at 5 branches'; the artifact gives a reader no way to tell whether this is the same pilot cohort under a different count, a subset of it, or a different group entirely, so the evidence offered for the revenue rebuttal cannot be checked against the pilot scope established earlier.

findings.evidence: This recommendation applies to items returned within 60 days of their due date; items still unreturned past that window remain subject to the existing replacement-cost billing process, matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established.
findings.fix: Either cite the pilot's day-by-day or cumulative return-timing data that shows returns clustering within 60 days, or drop the phrase claiming the cutoff matches a pilot pattern and state the 60-day boundary as an operational choice instead.
findings.location: Recommendation section, third paragraph (the 60-day scope sentence)
findings.violation: TOULMIN-GROUNDS is breached because the claim that the 60-day cutoff 'match[es] the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established' carries no attached evidence: the pilot description in 'What the Pilot Showed' reports only an aggregate 94-percent-versus-87-percent on-time-or-eventual return rate and never breaks returns down by days elapsed, so there is nothing in the artifact a reader could check this specific alignment against.

findings.evidence: Removing the financial penalty for late returns predictably increases both on-time return rates and overall program participation
findings.fix: Soften 'predictably increases' to something the grounds support, e.g. 'is associated with increases, in this pilot and in the cited multi-system review', or add the qualification that the effect is observed rather than law-like.
findings.location: Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide section, first paragraph
findings.violation: TOULMIN-QUALIFIER is breached because the unhedged modal force of 'predictably' asserts a general, reliable causal law, where the grounds actually behind it are a single 16-month pilot at half the consortium's branches plus one cited external brief that itself only reviewed return-rate outcomes, not participation outcomes; the claim's stated strength exceeds what those grounds establish.

findings.evidence: A skeptic on the board points to overdue fines as a source of materials-replacement funding, and argues that eliminating them systemwide will leave a shortfall the consortium has not planned for.
findings.fix: Add a paragraph addressing whether ending fines is expected to affect how long items stay checked out within the 60-day window, and what the pilot's renewal or hold-fulfillment data (if tracked) shows about that risk.
findings.location: Addressing the Revenue Concern section (the only rebuttal in the document)
findings.violation: TOULMIN-REBUTTAL is breached in part because the artifact answers the revenue objection but raises and answers no other objection, leaving a second foreseeable one unaddressed: the recommendation removes any escalating penalty for holding an item for up to 60 days, and the artifact's own opening section flags renewal-rate and checkout-volume monitoring as something the consortium already tracks, yet nowhere does the argument consider or answer whether removing the fine deterrent lengthens how long patrons keep items within that 60-day window, reducing availability of in-demand items for other patrons.
